units.title: Religion and belief systems in Australia after 1945

points.title: Aboriginal spiritualities and dispossession
points.brief: For Aboriginal peoples, separation from land, including through the Stolen Generations, cut connections with the Dreaming, kinship and ceremony.

points.title: Land rights and native title
points.brief: The Mabo decision (1992) and the Native Title Act 1993 recognised some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander connections to land, which are spiritual as well as legal.

points.title: The changing religious pattern
points.brief: Since 1945, migration has made Australia more religiously diverse, Christian affiliation has fallen, and the number reporting no religion has risen sharply.

points.title: Ecumenism and interfaith dialogue
points.brief: Ecumenism is Christian churches working together, as in the Uniting Church formed in 1977. Interfaith dialogue builds understanding between different religions.

points.title: Reconciliation and the churches
points.brief: Many churches have apologised for their role in removing Aboriginal children and support reconciliation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

points.title: A significant person in Buddhism
points.brief: Figures such as the Dalai Lama, Thich Nhat Hanh or Ashoka shaped Buddhism through their teaching and example.

points.title: Buddhist bioethics
points.brief: Buddhist views on issues such as euthanasia and IVF draw on the precept against harming life, compassion and the intention behind an act.

points.title: Buddhist environmental ethics
points.brief: Interdependence and compassion for all living beings lead many Buddhists to care for the environment.

points.title: Buddhist sexual ethics
points.brief: The third precept, to avoid sexual misconduct, asks Buddhists to avoid causing harm in relationships. Teachers and schools apply it differently.

points.title: A significant Buddhist practice
points.brief: Practices such as temple puja, the festival of Wesak or pilgrimage to sites linked to the Buddha express Buddhist beliefs.

points.title: A significant person in Christianity
points.brief: Figures such as Paul of Tarsus, Martin Luther or Catherine McAuley shaped Christianity through their beliefs and actions.

points.title: Christian bioethics
points.brief: Christian views on issues such as euthanasia and IVF draw on the sanctity of life and the dignity of each person, and differ between churches.

points.title: Christian environmental ethics
points.brief: Many Christians see people as stewards of God's creation, responsible for caring for it.

points.title: Christian sexual ethics
points.brief: Christian teaching on sexuality draws on scripture and church tradition, and churches differ on questions such as same-sex relationships.

points.title: A significant Christian practice
points.brief: Practices such as baptism or the marriage ceremony mark a person's relationship with God and the church.

points.title: A significant person in Hinduism
points.brief: Figures such as Shankara or Mahatma Gandhi shaped Hindu thought and practice through their teaching and lives.

points.title: Hindu bioethics
points.brief: Hindu views on issues such as euthanasia draw on ahimsa, karma and the duty to preserve life.

points.title: Hindu environmental ethics
points.brief: Belief that the divine is present in all things and the value of ahimsa lead many Hindus to respect nature.

points.title: Hindu sexual ethics
points.brief: Hindu teaching places sexuality within marriage and dharma, and views vary across communities.

points.title: A significant Hindu practice
points.brief: Practices such as puja, the marriage ceremony or pilgrimage to sites such as Varanasi express Hindu beliefs.

points.title: A significant person in Islam
points.brief: Figures such as the scholar al-Shafi'i or the Prophet's wife Aisha shaped Islamic law and tradition.

points.title: Islamic bioethics
points.brief: Islamic views on issues such as euthanasia and IVF draw on the belief that life belongs to God and on sharia.

points.title: Islamic environmental ethics
points.brief: Muslims see people as khalifa, trustees of God's creation, responsible for caring for it.

points.title: Islamic sexual ethics
points.brief: Islam places sexual relationships within marriage and values modesty, as taught in the Quran and Hadith.

points.title: A significant Islamic practice
points.brief: Practices such as Friday prayer at the mosque or the hajj pilgrimage express Islamic beliefs and community.

points.title: A significant person in Judaism
points.brief: Figures such as Moses Maimonides or Rabbi Hillel shaped Jewish thought and practice.

points.title: Jewish bioethics
points.brief: Jewish views on issues such as euthanasia and IVF draw on the value of preserving life and on rabbinic interpretation.

points.title: Jewish environmental ethics
points.brief: The idea that the earth belongs to God and the rule against needless destruction guide Jewish care for the environment.

points.title: Jewish sexual ethics
points.brief: Jewish teaching values sexuality within marriage, and the different movements in Judaism interpret the rules differently.

points.title: A significant Jewish practice
points.brief: Practices such as synagogue services, the marriage ceremony or customs of death and mourning express Jewish beliefs.

points.title: Inner peace and world peace
points.brief: Religions teach paths to inner peace, such as prayer and meditation, and see inner peace as a basis for peace between people.

points.title: Peace in Buddhism and Hinduism
points.brief: Buddhism teaches peace through overcoming craving and practising compassion. Hinduism teaches ahimsa and the peace of union with Brahman.

points.title: Peace in Christianity
points.brief: Christians follow Jesus's teaching to love enemies and be peacemakers, and many churches work for peace and justice.

points.title: Peace in Islam and Judaism
points.brief: Islam teaches that peace comes from submission to God. Judaism values shalom, peace with wholeness, and pursuing justice.

points.title: Religious contributions to peace
points.brief: Religious groups and leaders have worked for peace through interfaith dialogue, aid and campaigns against war.

points.title: Religious expression today
points.brief: People increasingly express spirituality outside traditional institutions, and new religious movements have formed.

points.title: Non-religious worldviews
points.brief: Atheism rejects belief in God, agnosticism holds that it cannot be known, and humanism finds meaning in human reason and values.

points.title: The rise of no religion in Australia
points.brief: In the 2021 census, close to two in five Australians reported no religion, a sharp rise over recent decades.

points.title: Religious and non-religious worldviews compared
points.brief: Worldviews differ on the source of meaning, the basis of ethics and life after death, but can share values such as care for others.

points.title: Responses of religious traditions
points.brief: Religions respond to non-religion through dialogue, outreach and by adapting how they engage with society.
